in_scope.title: Site Isolation is Dead: How Site Isolation is Broken in Agentic Browsers and Extensions
in_scope.title_norm: site isolation is dead how site isolation is broken in agentic browsers and extensions
in_scope.grounding: full-text (author-hosted S&P'26 PDF, open access). Read in full: abstract, S1, S2/S2.1 incl. Table 1, S4 (S4.1 MPI + Table 2, S4.3 scenarios, S4.4 feasibility study), S5 preamble + S5.1 opening, S5.4 guardrail design/evaluation incl. Table 3, S6 Discussion. NOT read line-by-line: S3 threat model, S4.2 SLI mechanism, S5.2, S5.3, S7 related work, S8, Appendix Tables 4-7. NOTE: the word 'Electron' NEVER appears in the paper (grep-confirmed) - targets are Chromium-based agentic browsers (BrowserOS, Vibe) and 7 Chrome extensions. ADJACENT tag reflects that the vulnerability class - a privileged process accepting forged IPC from a compromised renderer with no origin check - is structurally identical to Electron's renderer<->main / ipcMain trust problem, but the paper makes no Electron claim. Table 2 per-cell values were read as flattened PDF text and reconstructed from S4.1 prose; re-verify before quoting individual cells.
in_scope.why_it_matters: Closest thing in the ledger to a published, end-to-end demonstration that renderer->privileged-process IPC trust failure defeats process isolation in a real desktop application family. Key numbers: 9 systems analyzed (2 open-source agentic browsers + 7 Chrome extensions), ALL vulnerable to MPI and/or SLI; WebPilot the only MPI-immune one, and only because it exposes no risky actions. Renderer RCE chained from CVE-2025-0291 + Chromium Issue 379140430 on Chromium 130.0.6723.160, then forged Mojo IPC at the C++ level - site isolation bypassed WITHOUT an additional sandbox escape. Guardrail: IPI ASR 0.89 -> 0.00 (BrowserOS) and 0.52 -> 0.00 (Nanobrowser), TSR 0.20 -> 0.14 and 0.27 -> 0.29 on 100 WebArena tasks.

in_scope.title: From Documentation to Zero-day Vulnerabilities: LLM-Driven Fuzzing of JavaScript Engines in PDF Readers
in_scope.title_norm: from documentation to zero-day vulnerabilities llm-driven fuzzing of javascript engines in pdf readers
in_scope.grounding: FULL-TEXT as of 2026-08-23. arXiv:2608.06641v2 (18 Aug 2026) PDF fetched successfully (103,792 chars / 1,616 lines) and read end-to-end: abstract, S1-S10, Tables 1-4, Listings 1-5, Figure 1 caption. v2 is the CAMERA-READY and carries the ACM DOI 10.1145/3830454.3832609 and ISBN 979-8-4007-2871-6/2026/11 in the copyright block - this supersedes yesterday's 'ACM DOI not yet assigned'. Provenance recipe that worked: WebSearch the paper TITLE -> fetch arxiv.org/abs/... (which places the /pdf/ URL in the provenance set) -> fetch arxiv.org/pdf/... . A direct /pdf/ fetch as the first call is rejected ('URL not in provenance set'). STILL UNREAD/UNREADABLE: Figure 2 (six coverage curves; only axis ranges survive PDF-to-text flattening - no curve value may be quoted); Table 1 rows for IDs 10-14 and 26-28 are ELIDED as '...' in the extracted text, so eight vulnerabilities' per-ID type/impact/status are unavailable; the reference list was read only far enough to resolve the key citations.
in_scope.why_it_matters: Structurally the same target class as Electron - a native desktop application that embeds a JavaScript engine and exposes a large DOCUMENTED privileged host API to attacker-supplied script - and it turns the vendor's own API manual into both the grammar AND the inter-call constraint system that drives discovery. FULL-TEXT-GROUNDED numbers: targets Adobe Acrobat Reader v24.005.20421, Foxit PDF Reader v2024.4.0.27683, PDF-XChange Editor v10.5.2.395; DynamoRIO basic-block coverage, 5 independent 24h runs per tool per target; 2-week vulnerability campaign, crashes caught by werfault.exe, manually triaged; VM = 4 cores/8GB/Windows 8.1, crashes re-verified on Win10 22H2 + Win11 24H2. Coverage: up to 48% over Cooper (the source of the abstract's headline), 37% over TypeOracle, 19% over TypeOracle+Cooper, 17% over TypeOracle+Favocado, 15% over Favocado, 16-49% over Claude-3.7-Sonnet. Vulnerabilities: 57 crashing inputs (23 Adobe / 24 Foxit / 10 PDF-XChange) dedup by normalized call-stack signature to 31 unique zero-days; 11 potentially ACE; 26 of 31 fixed; 10 CVEs assigned; $2,450 bounty on TWO vulnerabilities (not on 26). THE KEY NUMBER FOR THIS THESIS: Table 1 aggregated row shows candidate-relationships-only finds 12 vulnerabilities while strong symbolic relationships find 28 and PDFuzzer-full 31 - i.e. co-occurrence is not enough, parameter-value constraints and ordering are what surface the bugs. Relationship distribution (Table 2, n=1,019): value-constraint 887 (87.0%), producer-consumer 69 (6.8%), implicit 63 (6.2%) - a producer-consumer-only model, the assumption behind most prior API fuzzers, misses ~93%. Instantiation success (Table 3, 71,586 invocations over 1,000 PDFs): 91.5% overall, value-constraint 95.1%, producer-consumer 81.5%, IMPLICIT ONLY 64.0%. Scale: 666 API functions / 886 parameters (435 documented fns + 507 params; 231 undocumented fns + 379 params); brute-force pair analysis would be 221,445 pairs x ~30s = >1,845 hours, hence the two-stage RAG design. LLM accuracy: spec inference 94% (82/87 params), grammar generation 97% APIs / 98% params, relationship inference 93% (56/60). Cost: $60.77 (GPT-4o) end-to-end vs $76.14-$174.83 for naive LLM; throughput ~3/s strong-relationship test cases, up to 20/s regular. LLM choice is near-irrelevant (<1% coverage difference on Adobe). The word 'Electron' NEVER appears in the full text (grep-confirmed, along with 'browser', 'Chromium', 'Node.js', 'desktop'); the Electron mapping is this watch's analysis. GAPS IT LEAVES OPEN for a discovery thesis: (1) single-process engine memory safety only - no cross-process propagation (Electron renderer->main IPC); (2) closed-source commercial targets force black-box fuzzing with DynamoRIO, whereas Electron app source usually sits readable inside the asar, leaving room for static+symbolic hybrid extraction; (3) a single fixed input source (the document file) - no multi-source problem of the kind Buzz to Boom's taxonomy describes; (4) the evaluation deliberately holds the fuzzing LOOP constant (TypeOracle's wrapper, no coverage-guided feedback) so it compares generators only and says nothing about feedback-driven fuzzers; (5) S8's 'generalization beyond PDF' is a FEASIBILITY STUDY ONLY - 2,925 Word VBA APIs / 3,768 parameters extracted from 5,920 pages of docs and CFGs built, but NO fuzzing run and no results. Best single hook for the thesis: implicit (state-mediated) relationships are the type this paper instantiates WORST (64.0%), and they are precisely the DOMINANT form of Electron IPC channel dependency (login -> session handle -> file access).
cves_visible_in_table1: CVE-2026-3777 (Foxit, UAF, ACE - the running-example popUpMenuEx/search.query bug)
in_scope.known_oddity: Table 4 Dimension 3 on Foxit: PC-Only (397,916 bbks) scores BELOW None (406,448), i.e. producer-consumer-only modelling appears to underperform no relationship modelling at all. The paper does not comment. Do not build an argument on the Dim-3 sub-rows without re-reading them in the published ACM version.

in_scope.title: Why Not Fix It Once and for All? An Empirical Study of Multiple Patches for Vulnerability Fixes in Open-Source Software
in_scope.title_norm: why not fix it once and for all an empirical study of multiple patches for vulnerability fixes in open-source software
in_scope.grounding: full-text (arXiv HTML preprint v1). Read in full: S3 Data Collection, S4 incl. Table 1 and S4.3, S5 Contributing Factors, S6 incl. Tables 2-4, S7 incl. Tables 5-7, S8 Related Work, S9 Discussion/Conclusion. NOT read line-by-line: S1 Introduction body, S4.1-S4.2 worked examples, Fig. 10 plotted values. Springer LNCS camera-ready does not exist yet (ESORICS is 14-18 Sep 2026), so all numbers are preprint numbers and author affiliations are unconfirmed.
in_scope.why_it_matters: The first systematic empirical study of MULTI-PATCH vulnerability fixes, and therefore the first venue-published quantification of the exact phenomenon this repo has documented qualitatively across two SiYuan XSS incomplete-fix chains. Key grounded numbers: 25,113 NVD CVEs with OSS security patches; 1,646 multi-patch (avg 2.55 patches/CVE); taxonomy A1=830 cross-branch/project, A2=30 in-branch multi-location, B1=16 workaround+fix, B2=128 fix+docs, C1=641 INCOMPLETE FIXES, C2=119 bug-introducing fixes; 127 CVE records mix vulnerability-INTRODUCING and vulnerability-FIXING commits under the same 'patch' label. CWE-79 XSS is the #1 CWE among multi-patch fixes at 519 CVEs; CWE-94 Code Injection enters the top 10 at #10, up 6 ranks vs single-patch. JavaScript is over-represented in multi-patch fixes (11.68% vs 9.53% single-patch, rank 3 in both); TypeScript 4.29% vs 3.56%. 31.7% of multi-patch fixes take more than a day end to end; for C1 specifically 336 <1d / 145 1-30d / 33 30-360d / 4 >360d. THE HEADLINE NEGATIVE RESULT: six vulnerability-detection models (CodeBERT, UniXcoder, PDBERT, LineVul, VulBERTa, Devign, ReVeal - LLMs deliberately excluded to avoid pre-training leakage) ALL score accuracy and F1 below 50% on incomplete-fix detection, which the authors call worse than random guessing; TPR drops 7.17-28.38 points vs single-patch data (CodeBERT 38.54->10.16, LineVul F1 75.36->5.46). Failure diagnosis: models assign the SAME label to pre-fix, intermediate and post-fix versions of a function. Clone detectors fail too: FIRE TPR 90.00->52.46, ReDebug 37.56->16.75, with FPR falling as well, i.e. they MISS rather than over-predict. Three uses for the thesis: (1) motivation - it forecloses the objection that the SiYuan incomplete-fix chains are just one badly-maintained project; (2) gap - the authors' own negative results open the detection gap that a sibling-sink-enumeration discovery method targets; (3) measurement-validity - their commit-ID de-duplication (URL count != patch count) and their finding that 5.8% of multi-patch records contain security-irrelevant patches is the same class of problem as this repo's 2026-09-02 correction that GHSA record counts are not discovery counts. CAUTION: the word 'Electron' never appears; JavaScript share is language-level only, with no Electron/npm breakdown. Cite as ADJACENT, never as Electron work.

in_scope.title: NatiSand: Native Code Sandboxing for JavaScript Runtimes
in_scope.title_norm: natisand native code sandboxing for javascript runtimes
authors: Marco Abbadini (Università degli studi di Bergamo)
Dario Facchinetti (Università degli studi di Bergamo)
Gianluca Oldani (Università degli studi di Bergamo)
Matthew Rossi (Università degli studi di Bergamo)
Stefano Paraboschi (Università degli studi di Bergamo)
in_scope.grounding: FULL TEXT. Read from the author-hosted CC-BY PDF (cs.unibg.it/seclab-papers/2023/RAID/natisand.pdf): abstract, §1 intro, §2 background (Landlock/eBPF/Seccomp), §3 security motivation + §3.1 threat model, §4 design objectives + architecture, §5 IPC policy detail, §6 nativeCall API, §7 experiments incl. Table 3 (32 CVEs, all rows), Table 4 (17 utilities, all rows), Table 5 (8 library ops, all rows), §8 related work, §9 conclusions + availability. NOT read as numbers: Figures 4 and 5 (latency/throughput plots for Benchmarks II and IV) — only the authors' stated '5 to 10 ms less latency' summary is available.
in_scope.why_in_scope: Config INCLUDE rule ('npm / supply-chain as it affects Electron or the Node.js runtime') plus the keywords.native_boundary_added_2026_09_06 axis (FFI, binding layer, native addon, memory safety). States the general fact an Electron threat model depends on: a JS runtime's permission system is a JS-only reference monitor, so any binary or shared library the runtime executes runs with the full privileges of the user running the whole application. Electron's main process is a Node.js runtime that loads .node addons directly. Sits alongside Mininode (RAID'20), HODOR (CCS'23), NodeShield (CCS'25) as Node.js-runtime attack-surface DEFENSE work.
in_scope.headline_numbers: 32 high-severity CVE exploits blocked with no functionality loss and no application/dependency changes (25 ACE, 4 AFO, 3 LFI; ImageMagick, GraphicsMagick, OpenCV, FFmpeg, libjpeg-turbo, libsndfile, Ghostscript, SQLite, Git, ExifTool, TensorFlow, Sockeye, Lightning, Unzip, GNU Tar, UnRAR, POCO, Pip, OpenSSL, GNSockets); affected modules total 2.6M downloads/week on npm + deno.land/x. Benchmark I (17 Linux utilities, slowdown vs plain Deno): NatiSand 2.88x worst (b2sum) to 1.13x best (wget), vs Minijail 7.19x-1.18x and Sandbox2 9.37x-1.24x. Benchmark II: ~5-10 ms lower latency per microservice than Minijail/Sandbox2. Benchmark III (8 native-library ops): NatiSand 1.51x-9.61x vs Wasm 1.70x-13.34x; worst case libpng verify (NatiSand 9.61x, Wasm 13.34x). Platform: Ubuntu 22.04, Ryzen 3900X, 64GB RAM; implemented in Deno.
in_scope.gap_left_open: (1) Threat model explicitly excludes attacks on JavaScript code, so the Electron chain (renderer XSS -> contextIsolation/preload bypass -> main process -> native code) starts outside its assumptions. (2) Linux-only by construction (Landlock/eBPF/Seccomp); no portability path discussed for Windows/macOS, Electron's primary targets. (3) Confinement, not discovery — says nothing about where native components occur in shipped desktop apps or how they are reached. (4) Zero mentions of Electron in the full text.
in_scope.surfaced_by: Required domain-restricted topical sweep (allowed_domains = venue hosts), query 'JavaScript runtime native code boundary vulnerabilities' — the rotation slot added to config on 2026-09-06 after the Bilingual Problems miss.

in_scope.title: BinWrap: Hybrid Protection against Native Node.js Add-ons
in_scope.title_norm: binwrap hybrid protection against native node js add ons
in_scope.grounding: FULL TEXT. Read from the author-hosted CC-BY PDF (cs.brown.edu/people/vpk/papers/binwrap.asiaccs23.pdf): abstract, §1 intro, §2 background (Node.js/V8/NAN), §5 ecosystem study RQ1-RQ3 with all reported figures, §6 design (MPK/PKU + seccomp-BPF, thread separation), §7 implementation/platform, §8 evaluation EQ1-EQ3 incl. all four CVE case studies and Table 1 (all 20 add-ons + 2 applications), §10 conclusion. NOT read as numbers: Figures 5, 6, 7 (syscall-set sizes and per-package overhead are plotted, not tabulated) — only the stated ranges are available.
in_scope.why_in_scope: Config INCLUDE rule ('npm / supply-chain as it affects Electron or the Node.js runtime') plus the keywords.native_boundary_added_2026_09_06 axis (native addon, N-API, nan, node-addon-api, cross-language, memory safety). Directly targets the .node native add-ons that a packaged Electron app loads into its privileged main process, and supplies the best public quantification of that boundary's size in the npm ecosystem.
in_scope.headline_numbers: Ecosystem study over a full npm replication of 1,508,366 libraries: 63,381 (4.2%) depend on a NAN- or NAPI-based native module (45,708 NAN, 23,239 NAPI, 5,548 both); 76.7% have exactly one native dependency, only 99 libraries have ten. Reach: 8,148 NAN modules with dependents (avg 7.2, max 8,457 = node-sass) covering 58,778 packages; 5,762 NAPI modules with dependents (avg 6.6, max 2,322) covering 38,383 — 97,161 dependent packages in total. Evaluation funnel: 5,073 packages with a native dependency -> 4,201 installable -> 3,508 de-duplicated -> 400 with runnable tests -> 20 add-ons (+2 whole applications: Video Thumb Grid, Manta Minnow). Security: 4/4 CVE exploits blocked — CVE-2018-11499 (node-sass/libsass UAF, blocked by MPK/PKU), CVE-2018-18577 (libtiff via picha, MPK/PKU), CVE-2019-3822 (libcurl via node-libcurl ROP chain, blocked by seccomp denying execve), CVE-2020-28248 (png-img/libpng callback overwrite, seccomp). Syscalls: Node.js APIs need the same 62 across all 20 add-ons; 2-35 inherited per add-on; >~2/3 blockable except zeroMQ (114, network sockets). Overhead: 0.71%-10.40% macro; micro domain-transition cost 240x with futex, 80x with inline-ASM spinning. Platform: Node.js v8.9.4, Linux v5.4, 32GB RAM, no kernel modifications.
in_scope.gap_left_open: (1) Zero mentions of Electron; analyses npm packages and Node.js server applications, never a packaged desktop app. (2) Attack entry point is untrusted server-side input, not the Electron chain renderer XSS -> preload/IPC -> main process -> native addon. (3) Requires Intel MPK/PKU hardware and Linux — a concrete reason existing native-boundary defenses do not attach to Windows/macOS Electron builds. (4) Security evaluation rests on 4 memory-corruption CVEs in the DSO; says nothing about logic flaws in the JS wrapper. (5) Node.js v8.9.4 (2017-era) — modern-Node applicability untested.
in_scope.surfaced_by: Reference [14] in the NatiSand (RAID'23) related-work section, chased to its venue. Confirms the standing practice of mining the related-work sections of newly-found in_scope papers for further venue hits.

in_scope.title: Too Much of a Good Thing: (In-)Security of Mandatory Security Software for Financial Services in South Korea
in_scope.title_norm: too much of a good thing in security of mandatory security software for financial services in south korea
in_scope.grounding: FULL TEXT of the USENIX cycle-1 PREPUBLICATION PDF (sec25cycle1-prepub-286-yun_0.pdf), read end-to-end through Section 8 Related Work and Section 9 Conclusion. NOT read: Appendices A-D (historical background, extra survey responses, HoaxEliminator sample output, additional issues). Tables 1 and 4 render as unlabelled mark grids in the extracted text, so the per-product threat-model mapping (which of T1-T4 applies to which PRODUCT) and the per-vulnerability Patched/Mitigated status are NOT reliably recoverable from this note. Word 'Electron' does not occur in the paper.
in_scope.why_in_scope: Config INCLUDE rules 'hybrid web/desktop apps' and 'DOM-based / XSS->RCE escalation into local privileges in desktop apps'. KSA 2.0 is the inverse architecture of Electron — a privileged native desktop process exposed to arbitrary web pages through a localhost HTTP/WebSocket API — and produces the same failure catalogue (origin/trust confusion, chained-API RCE, security-control bypass), which is the strongest available evidence that the vulnerability class is architectural rather than Electron-specific.
in_scope.headline_numbers: 7 mandatory KSA products (PRODUCT A-G, anonymised at a Korean government agency's request) covering all 17 top-tier Korean banks; 19 vulnerabilities. Four threat models derived from bind address / protocol / Origin verification: T1 remote attacker, T2 malicious website, T3 MitM via SSL stripping, T4 origin spoofer (justified by 196 renderer exploits vs 5 sandbox escapes in 2022). RCE in PRODUCT B by chaining SetLogoPath (files <=256 bytes bypass digital-signature validation, written to a fixed location, not deleted) with DecFileData (unvalidated output path). Anti-keylogging in PRODUCT D/E convertible into a system-wide keylogger by forcing symmetric encryption or disabling encryption. 5 memory-corruption bugs on Linux via AFLnet/AFL++ (PRODUCT F: 1 buffer overflow; PRODUCT G: 2 buffer overflows, 1 null deref, 1 segfault). Every KSA installs its own root CA; 5 of 7 do not remove it on uninstall; PRODUCT E's root-CA private key recovered from the installer binary and used to sign a certificate for google.com. Survey n=400 (demographically matched, chi-square gender 0.64 df=1 p>0.99, age 2.31 df=4 p>0.99): 97.35% of banking users had installed KSA, 59.25% did not understand its functions, only 14.75% knew it runs continuously, 0 participants identified the anomaly-detection/fingerprinting capability, 20.75% had never uninstalled, authors conclude 86.5% remain exposed after attempted removal. Desktop analysis n=48 via HoaxEliminator: mean 9.06 KSA programs installed per machine (SD 6.96, max 24), mean 4.1 of the studied products (SD 2.92), 27 of 48 running versions from 2022 or earlier, oldest install 2019-02-15. PRODUCT E shipped by 9 institutions at 9 different versions spanning 2019-02-20 to 2023-08-22.
in_scope.gap_left_open: (1) Electron, Chromium, CEF and WebView are never mentioned; the target is a native local server OUTSIDE the browser, not an embedded browser inside a desktop app. (2) KSA at least has an explicit (if weak) boundary — the HTTP Origin header; Electron's preload/contextBridge has no equivalent, and its exposed surface is hand-written IPC channels. (3) Discovery method is manual reverse engineering of 7 products plus protocol fuzzing — no automated or scalable discovery technique is proposed, which is exactly the space a discovery thesis occupies. (4) Memory-corruption bugs were found on Linux builds; applicability to the Windows builds nearly all Korean users run is not stated. (5) Products are anonymised, so findings cannot be tied to named vendors or independently re-verified.
in_scope.surfaced_by: Required domain-restricted topical sweep, query 'sandbox escape desktop application untrusted web content renderer' (allowed_domains = the six venue hosts). Second consecutive backfill miss found by this channel and by no other: the title contains none of the config keywords.

in_scope.why_in_scope: Config INCLUDE rule 'npm / supply-chain as it affects Electron or the Node.js runtime'. The canonical statement of the ambient-authority problem that an Electron main process inherits wholesale — every imported library holds all built-in APIs, globals, process.env, the module cache and require — and the missing middle link between Mininode (RAID'20) and HODOR (CCS'23) / NodeShield (CCS'25), all already in_scope.
in_scope.headline_numbers: Applied to over 1,000 npm libraries. SECURITY (Q1): attack set built from all Snyk npm vulnerabilities filtered to arbitrary code execution / RCE / sandbox escape = 132 candidates, minus 23 for other platforms or languages and 33 misclassified, yielding 63 working PoC attacks; Mir mitigates 61/63. The two failures are a package applying its own complex runtime wrapping, and typed-function manipulating the Function prototype chain. PRIVILEGE REDUCTION (Q2, 81 libraries = 31 usable Q1 libraries + 50 with extensive test suites): average 143.48x, range 3.5x-706x; permissions per library 2-658 (avg 42.2), split 1-341 R (avg 22.1), 0-29 W (avg 3.3), 0-209 X (avg 12.5), 0-87 I (avg 4.1); after Mir only 1 of 81 libraries retains security-critical system-wide permissions and only 5 retain security-concerning library-specific ones. COMPATIBILITY (Q3): 3,400 of 3,431 unique field-access locations (99.09%); 226,497 of 226,553 repeated accesses (99.98%); 73 of 81 packages fully compatible (90.12%); 2,541 of 2,557 test cases (99.37%). ABLATION: static analysis alone drops locations to 2,422 (70.59%) and packages to 58 (71.60%), and average inferred permissions from 155.9 to 42.3 — the import-time dynamic phase is what makes it usable (example: fs-promise computes fs wrappers by traversal). PERFORMANCE (Q4): 2.1s static analysis per library; 1.93% (approx 3.3ms) runtime enforcement overhead; accessed fields are hot, avg 795 accesses each. DEBLOATING COMPARISON (Q5): Mininode v.f604d9e takes 0.82-4.013s with no runtime overhead but fails on 7/88 libraries (5 entry-point, 1 dynamic-import, 1 OOM) and ALL 63/63 PoC attacks still succeed. Implementation: analysis mostly in Java, runtime in ~2.8 KLoC JavaScript on top of Lya.
in_scope.gap_left_open: (1) THE DECISIVE ONE — Section 3 'Non-threats' states Mir 'does not consider native libraries written in lower-level languages, such as C/C++, or libraries available in binary form', because they cannot be analysed by source-level static analysis AND can bypass a runtime protection that depends on memory safety. That single sentence is the door an Electron app's .node add-ons walk through, and it is the natural lead-in to Cross-Language Attacks (NDSS'22), Bilingual Problems (USENIX Sec'23), BinWrap (AsiaCCS'23) and NatiSand (RAID'23). (2) Also excluded: input-sanitization / command-injection attacks on APIs the library already uses; availability, DoS and side channels. (3) All evaluation is server-side Node.js/npm — no packaged desktop app, no renderer process, no IPC channel. (4) Attack entry point is 'inputs passed to a library', not remote web content. (5) 2021-era Node; exact version not stated in the sections read.

in_scope.title: Cross-Language Attacks
in_scope.title_norm: cross language attacks
in_scope.grounding: FULL open-access NDSS PDF (2022-78-paper.pdf). Read directly: abstract, Section I introduction, the threat-model composition and Language Transfer node construction, the CLA taxonomy (Rust bounds-check bypass, lifetime bypass, double free via FFI, return-address corruption, intended FFI interactions, concurrency), and the Firefox quantification tables. Read only in part: Sections V-VII, incl. the generalisation discussion to Go and other language combinations. NOT read: Appendix A (Go code samples). The attack-variant vs defeated-mechanism table renders as rows of quotation marks and is NOT reliably recoverable; the 'Dynamic calls' metric row was cut off and has no numbers.
in_scope.why_in_scope: Config keywords.native_boundary_added_2026_09_06 axis ('cross-language', 'language boundary', 'foreign function interface', 'ffi', 'memory safety'). Supplies the general mechanism — that a safe language's checks and an unsafe language's mitigations break DIFFERENT exploit stages and make mutually incompatible assumptions at the boundary — on which the whole JS<->C/C++ line in this ledger (Bilingual Problems, BinWrap, NatiSand) implicitly rests but which none of them states.
in_scope.headline_numbers: Firefox binary-level static analysis. Functions: Rust 487,763 (26.68% of binary), C/C++ 1,340,347 (73.32%), total 1,828,110. Call sites: Rust 327,653 (9.23%), C/C++ 3,220,415 (90.77%), total 3,548,068. Language transfer points: 227,896 = 6.42% of all call sites, of which Rust 12,118 (3.70% of Rust call sites, 5.32% of all transfer points) and C/C++ 215,778 (6.70%, 94.68%). Indirect calls: 280,441 = 7.90% of call sites, of which Rust 179,598 — 54.81% of Rust's own call sites and 64.04% of the binary's indirect calls — versus C/C++ 100,843 (3.13%, 35.96%). Scope restriction that makes the result non-trivial: the unsafe side HAS mitigation applied (e.g. CFI) and the safe side contains NO unsafe code of its own, so the vulnerability is the boundary itself rather than a stray 'unsafe' block. Rust deploys no shadow stack (being memory-safe), so C/C++ can corrupt the return address of a previously-called Rust function and it is never checked. Go's GC costs approximately 25% CPU utilization depending on workload. Named real deployments motivating the work: Firefox (Servo CSS style calculation, Dogear, MP4 metadata parser, neqo QUIC), Tor, Windows, Fuchsia, Linux flavours (Rust); Docker, Kubernetes, CockroachDB, BoltDB (Go).
in_scope.gap_left_open: (1) The safe languages studied are Rust and Go — the JavaScript/V8 <-> C/C++ boundary is NOT analysed, and it differs in kind: no ownership checks, no compile-time bounds checks, instead a GC and V8 heap structure, with transfer points of a different shape (N-API type conversions, handle scopes, callbacks). (2) Measured on ONE browser binary; zero packaged Electron apps. (3) The Firefox analysis counts structural preconditions statically — it does not demonstrate an exploitable bug in Firefox and must not be cited as if it did. (4) 2022 measurement; Firefox's Rust share has certainly moved since. Porting CLA to Electron's .node boundary — counting transfer points and constructing an actual chain — is an open, directly claimable contribution.

in_scope.title: Are your Sites Truly Isolated? Automatically Detecting Logic Bugs in Site Isolation Implementations
in_scope.title_norm: are your sites truly isolated automatically detecting logic bugs in site isolation implementations
in_scope.found_via: author/lab-page mining of the TU Braunschweig Institute for Application Security publications page (Musch/Johns, author target #1 from next_targets_2026_09_17)
in_scope.grounding: full-text PDF (NDSS open access). Read in full: abstract, S1 Introduction, S2-A Background, S3 Vulnerability Analysis and Classification (all three classes + three case studies), opening of S4 Fuzzer Design, S6 Evaluation A-E in full, opening of S7 Discussion, S8 Related Work, opening of S9. NOT read line-by-line: bulk of S4 (generator design), all of S5 Fuzzer Implementation, rest of S7, appendix Table V (full 39-bug list). No coverage percentage is quoted because Fig. 7 gives them only as a plot.
in_scope.why_it_matters: The first automated discovery method targeting the renderer->privileged-process IPC boundary under an explicit COMPROMISED-RENDERER threat model - the post-XSS state of an Electron renderer. Grounded numbers: 1,328 bug reports examined by hand -> 39 genuine Site Isolation bypasses in Chrome+Firefox, classified into missing checks (most common), bypassed checks (4 reports) and origin confusion; the decisive empirical observation is that nearly all vendor-accepted PoCs need only that the renderer circumvent renderer-side checks and SPOOF ORIGIN-RELATED PARAMETERS IN OUTGOING IPC MESSAGES, which is what makes IPC-message mutation a sufficient model of compromise. Method: patch the browser's IPC-bindings generator to add hooks, mutate outgoing messages (IPCFuzzer JS API), generate inputs from the browser's own Web IDL, and detect bugs with two process-level oracles - a leak sanitizer (magic string seeded in victim-site storages, flagged when it reaches the attacker process) and a process sanitizer (cross-site process reuse). Semantic validity 89.5% Chrome / 85.3% Firefox. Time-to-trigger on three known Chrome bugs: CVE-2019-5856 <1 min, CVE-2018-18345 ~14 min, CVE-2022-1637 (origin confusion) 11.4 h - a three-order-of-magnitude spread driven by precondition complexity, not search space. Oracles: 3/5 sampled PoCs caught by the leak sanitizer, 1/5 by the process sanitizer, overall false-negative rate 12.5% and ZERO false positives by construction (the generator knows each document's ground-truth site). Month-long campaign (2 weeks each on Chromium 127.0.6497.0 and Firefox 121.0, AMD EPYC 7702P 128 cores / 500 GB, 50 parallel Docker instances) found FOUR bugs: Window.name not reset cross-site (Chrome, S4, #384781865); visited-URL broadcast for :visited styling (Firefox, S3, #1938107); missing CORB (Firefox, S3, #1532642); and history origin confusion via renderer-side-only check on history.replaceState (Firefox, S2, CVE-2024-9392, $8,000 bounty) whose PoC is four lines of JS. 8.7% (Chrome) / 13.1% (Firefox) of iterations ended with the browser process killing the renderer for misbehaviour. USE AS BOTH MOTIVATION AND CONTRAST: motivation because it legitimises automated attack of the post-compromise IPC surface; contrast because a browser process re-validates every renderer claim BY DESIGN (process lock, site tracking) and finding bugs in that logic is the contribution, whereas an Electron main process exposes application-defined ipcMain handlers with no process lock, no site notion and frequently no origin check - so the transferable gap is precisely (a) what plays the role of the ground-truth invariant that gave this paper 0% FPR, and (b) what plays the role of Web IDL when the IPC surface is per-app string channels. CAUTION: the word 'Electron' does not appear and every target is Chrome or Firefox; cite as ADJACENT browser methodology, never as Electron evidence.
in_scope.scope_consistency_note: Admitted while 'Isolated and Exhausted' (USENIX Sec'23) and 'State of Browser Process-Isolation: The Same-Site Weakness' (S&P'26) remain EXCLUDED. The distinction: those two are measurements/attacks about browser SI; this one contributes a reusable DISCOVERY TECHNIQUE at the renderer<->privileged-process IPC boundary, the same ground on which Favocado and COOPER were admitted for the engine-binding boundary. Apply this distinction to any further SI paper.

in_scope.title: REFLECTA: Reflection-based Scalable and Semantic Scripting Language Fuzzing
in_scope.found_via: AsiaCCS 2025 (Hanoi) title-by-title venue-year sweep, Cycle 1 accepted-papers page
in_scope.grounding: full text, author-hosted PDF (hexhive.epfl.ch). Read closely: abstract, S1, Table 1, S6 Evaluation (setup + Table 3 + S6.2/Table 4 + S6.3 opening + S6.4/Table 6/Fig.9), S7, S8, S9. NOT read line-by-line: S2, S3, S4.1-4.3 internals, S5 Implementation, Appendices A-G. No raw edge counts quoted because Fig.6 gives coverage only as plots.
in_scope.why_it_matters: The strongest existing demonstration that a fuzzer can recover a scripting engine's callable API surface AT RUNTIME FROM ZERO SPECIFICATION, using reflection alone - the capability an Electron auditor needs because the bridge API (contextBridge objects, ipcMain string channels) is per-application and specified nowhere. Grounded numbers: 6 engines / 4 languages (CRuby, MRuby, CPython, MicroPython, PHP, V8). Specification budget 83-91 LoC grammar and ZERO symbols per language, against Nautilus 8,719 rules + 8,655 symbols for PHP alone and Fuzzilli 881 + 1,181 LoC for JavaScript. Semantic correctness average 62.3% vs Nautilus 35.7% and PolyGlot 20.2% (per-target: Ruby 61.0%, MRuby 62.5%, CPython 53.1%, MicroPython 62.1%, PHP 70.8%, V8 64.2%); Fuzzilli reaches 67.7% on V8 but only with 1,181 LoC of hand-written type annotation. Aggregate 1.74x correctness over Nautilus, 3.35x over PolyGlot; 1.63x / 2.21x edge coverage. 25 unique previously-unknown bugs, all developer-confirmed, 16 fixed: 8 MRuby, 14 MicroPython, 3 PHP (10 null-deref, 5 global-buf, 3 heap-buf, 3 heap-UAF, 2 segfault, 1 stack-overflow). Config: 16-core Xeon 5218 / 64 GB, one core per instance, 24 h x 8 repetitions with 95% CIs; 3-month bug campaign but every bug found within 24 h. THE DECISIVE NEGATIVE RESULT: ZERO new bugs in V8, because REFLECTA deliberately generates no control flow and so never makes code hot enough to reach the JIT pipeline - 'Reflecta primarily finds bugs in standard libraries'. Case study Fig.9 is a 4-line MRuby stack overflow that Nautilus and PolyGlot missed ONLY because filter_map and args= were absent from the hand-written grammar and the seed corpus, i.e. under-specification of the surface, not weak search, hid the bug. CITE AS MOTIVATION AND METHODOLOGICAL ANCESTOR, and for the asymmetry it leaves open: contextBridge-injected objects ARE reflectable from a renderer, but the set of ipcRenderer.invoke channel strings is NOT, because they are string keys.
in_scope.scope_consistency_note: Admitted while Fuzzilli (NDSS'23), Montage (USENIX'20) and 'Fuzzing JavaScript Engines with a Graph-based IR' (CCS'24) stay EXCLUDED. The line: those fuzz ENGINE INTERNALS / the JIT pipeline, where no host application sits on the other side of the surface; REFLECTA fuzzes the EXPOSED API SURFACE and says so itself (no control flow, no V8 JIT bugs, bugs in standard libraries). Same ground on which Favocado and COOPER were admitted. Apply this test to the next engine-fuzzing paper.
in_scope.caveats: The words Electron, Node.js, desktop and embedder never appear; V8 is fuzzed standalone, not as an embedded engine with host-injected objects. Ruby is built WITHOUT ASan (ASan build crashes), so CRuby bug sensitivity is not comparable. The PyRTFuzz comparison is explicitly best-effort on Python 3.9 after a Python 3.12 failure. SoFi could not be compared at all - not open source.
in_scope.title_norm: reflecta reflection based scalable and semantic scripting language fuzzing

in_scope.title: SoFi: Reflection-Augmented Fuzzing for JavaScript Engines
in_scope.pdf: PAYWALLED - ACM DL only; SMU InK mirror ink.library.smu.edu.sg/.../3460120.3484823.pdf returns an EMPTY body
in_scope.found_via: related-work mining of REFLECTA (AsiaCCS'25): SoFi is a column in its Table 1 and is named in S6.1 as the baseline that could not be compared. This is the 2026-09-12 sub-rule (grep a newly admitted paper's prose for TOOL NAMES it argues against) paying out.
in_scope.grounding: WEAK - ABSTRACT + SECONDARY SOURCES ONLY. Full text NOT read: ACM paywalled and the SMU institutional copy fetched empty. Every methodological statement comes from the published abstract; the two factual claims about its results come from (a) REFLECTA AsiaCCS'25 Table 1 / S6.1 and (b) SoK: Prudent Evaluation Practices for Fuzzing, IEEE S&P 2024, as summarised in search results rather than read from its PDF. NO NUMBER from SoFi's own evaluation is recorded anywhere, because none was readable.
in_scope.why_it_matters: The origin of reflection-based discovery of an object's UNSEEN attributes and methods as a fuzzing primitive for JavaScript, and the direct ancestor of REFLECTA. Its gap statement is the citable part: semantic-aware JS fuzzers of the day relied on manual rules that are 'labor-intensive, incomplete and engine-specific', and such fuzzers STRUCTURALLY CANNOT call a method absent from the seed corpus or the pre-defined rules. That is the exact condition of an Electron app's application-defined privileged surface. Method (from the abstract): fine-grained analysis to identify available variables and infer their types for mutation; automatic REPAIR of syntactically/semantically invalid test cases instead of discarding them; reflection-based analysis to surface unseen attributes and methods; claimed engine-general with no manual configuration.
in_scope.citation_warning: CITE THE TECHNIQUE, NOT THE RESULTS. SoK: Prudent Evaluation Practices for Fuzzing (Schloegel et al., IEEE S&P 2024) reports that ALL SEVEN vulnerabilities SoFi claimed in V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore were INVALID and rejected by the engine developers, six of the seven before the submission deadline. SoFi was also never open-sourced, so no independent comparison exists (REFLECTA S6.1). Read the S&P'24 SoK directly before repeating this.
in_scope.scope_consistency_note: Same admission ground as Favocado, COOPER and REFLECTA: a discovery technique for an UNSPECIFIED API surface. Fuzzilli / Montage / graph-based-IR JS fuzzing stay excluded as engine-internals work.

Determine whether SoFi's reflection runs inside the target engine or is reconstructed externally - decisive for transplanting the technique to an Electron renderer.
in_scope.title_norm: sofi reflection augmented fuzzing for javascript engines

excluded.title: FIDES: End-to-end Compartments for Mixed-language Systems
excluded.authors_first: Sai Venkata Krishnan (IIT Madras), Arjun Menon (InCore Semiconductors), Chester Rebeiro, KC Sivaramakrishnan (IIT Madras / Tarides)
excluded.fulltext_status: FULL TEXT READ (15-page author-hosted PDF). Disposition rests on the paper itself, not on an abstract.
excluded.surfaced_by: First-ever full sweep of the AsiaCCS 2026 accepted-papers list (Cycle 2), after the AsiaCCS channel was fixed this run.
excluded.reason: Hardware-assisted intra-process compartmentalisation for mixed OCaml-C applications: function-level code compartments plus hardware fat pointers, implemented on a MODIFIED Shakti RISC-V processor and evaluated on baremetal MirageOS unikernels (an electronic voting machine, 68K LoC, and an HTTPS server, 500K LoC). EXCLUDED, and the controlling precedent is the ledger's own standing bulk dismissal of 'the MPK/PKU and memory-isolation systems line' recorded under BinWrap's bibliography (Donky USENIX'20, PKRU-Safe EuroSys'22, ERIM, Jenny, xMP) together with the individual exclusions of Galeed (ACSAC'21) and Pitchfork (ACSAC'22). FIDES's own Table 4 places it squarely in that line - it benchmarks itself against Secage, Glamdring, GOTEE, Donky, Enclosures, PKRU-Safe, Galeed, CHERI-JNI, ACES, MINION and CHERIoT - so admitting it while excluding Galeed and PKRU-Safe would be inconsistent. The safe language is OCaml; there is no JavaScript engine, no Node.js, no npm and no desktop application anywhere in the paper, and the mechanism REQUIRES CUSTOM SILICON, so it can never be applied to an Electron app on commodity x86/ARM. Distinguish from 'Cross-Language Attacks' (NDSS'22), which IS in_scope ADJACENT: that paper is an attack TAXONOMY for the safe/unsafe boundary as a class, whereas this is one more hardware compartment mechanism. WORTH A MANUAL CITATION NONETHELESS, which is why this entry is long: section 3.2.2 gives the cleanest published illustration of a native component subverting a managed-language closure. C code calls caml_named_value to fetch two OCaml callbacks and overwrites the code pointer inside the 'sum' closure with that of the 'leak' closure; the write is WITHIN THE BOUNDS of the sum closure, so spatial memory safety does not stop it, and every later call to sum - including from OCaml - runs leak. That is structurally identical to what a malicious or buggy Node.js native addon can do to a JS function object across N-API, which is exactly the primitive a thesis on Electron native-addon risk needs a citable example of. PROMOTE TO in_scope ONLY IF the thesis adds a native-addon confinement chapter surveying compartmentalisation mechanisms irrespective of runtime.
excluded.grounding: Numbers read from the PDF: 6.1% LUT and 6.0% register area increase on a Xilinx Artix-7 AC701 FPGA with operating frequency unaffected, versus CHERIoT's >100% area increase; 1.9% average execution-time overhead for code compartments across the Computer Language Benchmarks Game suite; 36% average overhead for fat-pointer-hardened C; a 5.4x microbenchmark slowdown when a higher-order function is placed in a non-fluid separate compartment, which fluid compartments reduce to baseline; EVM case study 1.04x overhead at 6 fluid compartments rising to 1.19x without fluid compartments, with average compartment code size falling from 132KB to 47KB at 23 compartments; HTTPS server throughput 57 requests baseline vs 46 / 49 / 52 for the three compartmentalisation strategies (19.3% down to 8.8% loss); policy annotation cost 70 LoC for the 68K-LoC EVM and 250 LoC for the 500K-LoC web server; compiler changes 50+149+20 LoC in OCaml and 155+37 LoC in LLVM plus a 500-LoC fat-pointer pass.
excluded.bibliography_checked: YES, section 7 read in full. NIL new in_scope. Every watched-venue citation is already dispositioned or already bulk-dismissed under the memory-isolation line (Galeed ACSAC'21 excluded; Donky USENIX'20 and PKRU-Safe EuroSys'22 bulk-dismissed via BinWrap). The rest - CHERIoT, CHERI-JNI, ACES, MINION, Secage, Glamdring, GOTEE, CETIS, Enclosures, CCured, Delta Pointers, Low-Fat, SoftboundCETS, Checked-C, MarkUs, Dieharder - are non-venue or pre-2020. DO NOT RE-CHASE.

context_non_venue.title: Buzz to Boom: Detecting Message Progression Vulnerabilities in Electron Applications via Segmented Directed Fuzzing
context_non_venue.title_norm: buzz to boom detecting message progression vulnerabilities in electron applications via segmented directed fuzzing
context_non_venue.venue: arXiv (preprint)
context_non_venue.scope_topical: PRIMARY (Electron vulnerability discovery — most thesis-central out-of-venue item to date)
context_non_venue.why: Strongest out-of-venue candidate this watch has surfaced: a segmented directed fuzzing framework (Proton) that DISCOVERS zero-day vulnerabilities in real Electron apps — the exact thesis topic, not merely Node.js-runtime-adjacent. Defines a new bug class, Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs): attacker-controlled inputs that chain across processes via message passing to reach privileged/terminal sinks (OS command execution). Explicitly positions past prior Electron work (unsafe-config + malicious-DOM studies, i.e. DOM-tree type/Inspectron/COINDEF) as unable to detect these cross-process, multi-step exploits. Evaluated on 589 real Electron apps → 23 zero-day MPVs, 22 to full RCE (projects >50k GitHub stars), 13 acks / 11 fixes / 11 CVEs, Vercel bug bounty on Hyper; 17 more zero-days than end-to-end fuzzing.
context_non_venue.venue_status: arXiv-only v1 (22 Jul 2026), cs.CR. fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.mpv_definition_verbatim: S1: 'A noteworthy property of a Message Progression Vulnerability - differentiating it from existing ones - is the involvement of multiple Electron processes, leading to chaining two or more vulnerabilities through multi-step message passing, to the final consequence.' Prior message-related vulnerabilities 'only need at most one-step exploitation from one process to another.' This is the sharpest available statement of the gap the paper claims over the ledger's existing Electron corpus.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.gap_claim_against_prior_electron_work: S1: 'existing Electron security studies mainly focus on unsafe configuration checks, and mitigation of malicious Document Object Model (DOM) content, or unsafe cross-context communication. None of them detects the progression of attacker-controlled messages across multiple Electron processes, let alone MPV.' It further argues cross-context STATIC analyses 'struggle with the dynamic message construction and asynchronous message passing', and that existing DYNAMIC web fuzzers 'are monolithic and do not coordinate across Electron's process boundaries', wasting budget on 'inputs that fail to propagate past the first boundary'. Directly names the limitation of the config-auditing line (Inspectron) and the DOM line (NDSS'23 DOM-tree typing / COINDEF) that this ledger already holds in in_scope.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.motivating_example_paperlib: Figure 1 / S2.1, verbatim: a victim clicks a malicious 'paperlib://' URI embedded in a webpage (A), which triggers a chain of THREE vulnerabilities across Electron's processes via message passing - an unintended function invocation in the MAIN process (B), a client-side request forgery in the UTILITY process (C), and DOM-based XSS in the RENDERER (D) - ultimately yielding arbitrary command execution. Described as a 'four-step chain, spanning three Electron processes'. The CVE is redacted in the preprint as 'CVE-2025-XXXX'. Note the utility process: this is the only item in the whole ledger that treats Electron's UTILITY process as part of the attack surface.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.source_taxonomy_three_types: S2.2.2 defines exactly three payload sources, coded U/F/S in Table 1. (U) Custom URI - 'app://action?content=payload'; the OS invokes the Electron app and delivers the URI to its open-url handler. (S) Remote Server Response - attacker-controlled values flow to network APIs such as fetch; 'commonly arises when an intermediate vulnerability, such as a client-side request forgery (CSRF), happens', and 'commonly appears in applications supporting plugin installation, remote file loading, and MCP server imports'. (F) Local File Access - attacker-controlled values flow to fs.readFile or BrowserWindow.loadFile; verbatim: 'No prior file system compromise is required: an attacker can exploit browser auto-download to silently place a malicious file in the default downloads directory, then trigger a custom URI to cause the application to load it.' THESIS VALUE: this is a published, citable source taxonomy for Electron desktop apps, and it converges independently with the delivery channels this watch derived from vendor advisories (config/profile files, sync, export, LLM output) - both say the untrusted-input frontier of a desktop app is NOT the network request.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.sink_taxonomy_intermediate_vs_terminal: S2.2.3 + Table 1 caption, verbatim: 'intermediate sinks forward attacker-controlled data into a message destined for another process; terminal sinks directly cause the security consequence (e.g., OS command execution)', and 'a single API may act as either depending on the runtime context'. Intermediate sinks are also called Progression APIs and 'generalize the notion of message passing beyond explicit IPC' (S3), covering script execution, window navigation and custom protocol handlers, not just ipcRenderer/ipcMain. Conditionally-terminal APIs named: contents.executeJavaScript(T) and eval(T).
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.process_model_verbatim: S2.2.1: main process runs Node.js with full native API access; UTILITY processes are 'spawned by the main to handle background tasks such as network requests and file access, and ALSO run with Node.js access'; renderers display web content. Under the default secure configuration each renderer keeps two isolated JS contexts - the preload context (privileged: process, ipcRenderer; exposes selectively via contextBridge) and the main-world context (standard browser APIs + whatever preload exposed).
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.method_two_phases: Phase I: static progression analysis identifies candidate vulnerable paths and segment boundaries by reasoning about payload injection points, IPC message flows and dangerous API sinks. Phase II: coverage-guided fuzzing per segment with two objectives - reach a terminal sink in the current process, OR reach a Progression API that propagates the payload to the next process, in which case the produced message SEEDS THE CORPUS of the next segment. Halting per segment (S4.3): (i) terminal sink reached and PoC saved, (ii) branch coverage saturates with no new Progression API output for k iterations, or (iii) global time budget expires. Algorithm 1 also skips segments containing only INVERTIBLE operations and reconstructs their inputs afterwards by inversion.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.llm_role: LLMs are used as an AGENT inside the pipeline, not as the detector. Per S4.2 the agent must emit four artifacts per discovered path: (1) an analysis.md of sources/sinks/segment boundaries, (2) a dataflow-segments.json enumerating each segment with code location, process type and links to neighbours, (3) per-segment fuzzing harnesses, and (4) LLM-generated seeds for each segment's initial corpus (S4.3: 'one representative input per parse branch'). Appendix D (UNREAD) is titled 'Agent Design' with D.1 Taint Analysis and Segmentation Agent and D.2 Harness Synthesis Agent. The specific model name is NOT stated in the portion read.
fulltext_notes_2026-08-18.why_this_matters_to_the_thesis: This is now the best-grounded statement in the repo of the METHODOLOGICAL gap a discovery thesis can claim: config auditing (Inspectron) and DOM-content defenses (NDSS'23, COINDEF) are single-process and single-step; monolithic web fuzzers cannot cross Electron's process boundaries. It also supplies a ready-made vocabulary - sources U/F/S, Progression APIs, intermediate vs terminal sinks, segmentation boundaries - that a thesis can adopt or explicitly argue against. Caution: because it is arXiv-only it must be cited as a preprint, and S6's numbers should not be quoted until the evaluation section is actually read.

Takes a *differential* angle this watch has not seen at a watched venue — it compares Electron's implementation of web security mechanisms against Google Chrome's, using manual testing plus the Web Platform Tests (WPT) cross-browser suite, and reports significant divergences in CORS, permissions, cookie handling, and especially the notion of an *origin* for local (file://) HTML content and webviews. context_non_venue.title: Lost in Translation: Exploring the Risks of Web-to-Cross-platform Application Migration
context_non_venue.title_norm: lost in translation exploring the risks of web-to-cross-platform application migration
context_non_venue.venue: Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs / PETS) 2025(4), pp. 24-39
context_non_venue.scope_topical: PRIMARY (Electron framework security, differential analysis) — but PoPETs is NOT one of the 9 watched venues
context_non_venue.why: The strongest Electron-specific paper this watch has added since Inspectron, and the peer-reviewed publication of the UIC MS thesis previously ledgered above. It is the FOURTH discovery methodology in the Electron landscape this repo tracks, alongside black-box config auditing (Inspectron), defenses (NDSS'23 DOM-tree type, COINDEF) and directed fuzzing (Buzz to Boom): DIFFERENTIAL TESTING, using Chrome as the oracle for what a security mechanism is supposed to do and Electron as the system under test. Its framing sentence is the cleanest available statement of why this gap existed: 'unlike traditional browsers, Electron lacks a dedicated testing framework, leaving critical security mechanisms unexplored at scale.' METHOD: two phases — hand-written header tests across three embedding contexts (top-level / iframe / WebView) and two fetch modes (remote / local), Selenium-driven, 23 headers in Table 1; then a retrofit of the Web Platform Tests suite to Electron, using mitmproxy to capture WPT-server-resolved test pages, storing ONLY top-level frames locally (storing sub-resources locally would destroy the very policy under test), a new --local-files-path WPT runner argument, request rewriting via webRequest.onBeforeRequest in Electron and a purpose-built declarativeNetRequest extension in Chrome, then regex-based differential log analysis. SETUP: 8 Electron versions with matching Chromium builds spanning 2021-2024 (12.0.2/Ch89 through 31.3.0/Ch126, Table 3); WPT commit d92dadb2 pushed 2024-08-16; preliminary phase on Electron 30.0.6; MacBook Air M1 / macOS Sonoma 14.6, attacks additionally verified on Windows. Threat model: attacker script already inside the renderer, arriving via a compromised NPM package at build time, a dynamically loaded remote script, or a socially engineered file import. FINDINGS (Table 4, 8 divergences, 6 of them present in ALL tested versions): FOUR NEW — (1) SOP: Electron treats every local file as the SAME origin where Chrome assigns file:// a null origin, so an attacker-dropped local HTML file inherits the application's origin and privileges with no user interaction; the paper's PoC (Listing 3) navigates to ftp://user:psw@ftp.server, waits 5s, then iframes file:///Volumes/ftp.server/malicious.html — Electron permits automatic FTP, 'an attack vector explicitly blocked in modern browsers'. Stealthy on Windows (no system notification); on macOS an FTP prompt requires user approval. Consequences named: read other local files, fetch() system files, recover the logged-in username from absolute paths in logs, reach browser cookies and SSH keys. (2) CORS: cross-origin requests from a local file fail in Chrome and SUCCEED in Electron — local execution contexts are exempt, so with a nodeIntegration:true WebView an attacker bypasses the restriction with NO application-specific vulnerability required. (3) CSP: no CSP directive exists for file:// URLs and Electron does not extend enforcement to local files, so a strict CSP in an Electron app governs only remotely-served content. (4) HTTPS: no automatic HTTP->HTTPS upgrade, no native HSTS (must be done in a preload script), and WebViews do NOT enforce Mixed Content Blocking. THREE KNOWN-AND-UNFIXED — X-Frame-Options not applied to WebViews/WebContentViews (the paper is careful: this is DELIBERATE, for developer flexibility, not a bug); Permissions-Policy enforced only when the top-level document is remote, plus OS-level permissions granted to the WHOLE APPLICATION rather than per origin so every embedded page and WebView inherits camera/filesystem grants once the user allows them; cookie-jar desynchronisation from non-printable characters above ASCII 127 (stored but document.cookie returns empty) enabling subdomain-attacker session fixation. ONE FIXED — Electron 12.0.2 failed to enforce SameSite at all. REAL-WORLD STUDY, n=30 showcase apps instrumented with Puppeteer in debugging mode, explicitly reusing Inspectron's methodology: 25 of 30 load the main renderer from file:// (Local->Local 17, Local->Remote 8, Remote->Remote 5); of the 8 that mix, 3 pull in third-party analytics/consent/advertising/Google SSO and 2 embed remote iframes (one Cookiebot); 5 apps deploy a WebView and 3 of those 5 load local files INTO the WebView (named example: the Biscuit browser app, where a crafted file:// link delivered by message or email renders with full app privileges); Figma named as local-interface-plus-remote-fetch; 12 of 30 deploy a CSP and ALL TWELVE are judged insufficient because CSP cannot regulate local content, with Cacher having written every directive against the unsupported 'file:' scheme so the whole policy is silently ignored; VS Code is the one positive example, disabling file:// and registering a custom vscode:// scheme. DISCLOSURE: reported to Cacher and to the Electron team with PoCs; ELECTRON ACKNOWLEDGED AND DECLINED — the behaviours 'align with Electron's intended security model', file:// handling 'is intentional and documented', developers are expected to avoid such deployments — the same response Inspectron received. PROPOSAL (unimplemented): a new CSP directive file-src with keywords none / self / sha256- / nonce- / path-. WHY IT MATTERS TO THIS THESIS: (a) it supplies the amplification factor for every XSS->RCE advisory already in this ledger — if SiYuan, Notesnook, DbGate or Vikunja load their renderer from file://, a single XSS wins not just app-context execution but the entire local-file origin; (b) it is a direct methodological competitor if the thesis uses differential testing, and the delta must be stated explicitly — this paper tests FRAMEWORK policy semantics, not APPLICATION sinks, and its own 30-app analysis is static resource extraction only, with the authors conceding that 'runtime permission requests, API-level access, and WebView execution flows' are out of scope; (c) the authors themselves name automated code-retrofitting frameworks for web-to-Electron migration as the promising future direction, which is a gap left open on the record.

context_non_venue.title: Electron upstream security advisories, 2026 (two coordinated batches: CVE-2026-34764..34781 and CVE-2026-70597..70612)
context_non_venue.venue: Electron project / GitHub Security Advisories (GHSA), mirrored in the GitLab Advisory Database and NVD
context_non_venue.scope_topical: PRIMARY (Electron framework vulnerabilities) — but upstream CVEs, not peer-reviewed academic work
context_non_venue.why: Best-grounded real-world motivation material the watch has produced, and the first item that lets the thesis quantify the Electron framework's own vulnerability trend from an authoritative source. GLAD's npm/electron index lists 35 advisories dated 2026 versus 1 in 2025, 2 in 2024 and 5 in 2023 — a step change driven by two coordinated batch disclosures. Most thesis-relevant, all landing squarely on the boundaries this thesis targets: (a) CONTEXT-ISOLATION BYPASSES — CVE-2026-70601 (7.5 HIGH, CWE-693): apps exposing Promise-returning functions via contextBridge (the standard wrapper for ipcRenderer.invoke) let untrusted web content hijack Function.prototype.bind and reach the isolated preload world and every capability it holds, escalating to Node.js access where the renderer is unsandboxed or nodeIntegration is on; CVE-2026-70610 (5.4 MEDIUM, CWE-1321): the contextBridge object-copy path used v8::Object::Set ([[Set]] semantics) in CreateProxyForAPI (shell/renderer/api/electron_api_context_bridge.cc), so a crafted __proto__ property fired the inherited Object.prototype setter and polluted the prototype of objects landing in the privileged preload context — fixed by switching to CreateDataProperty ([[DefineOwnProperty]]), PR #51083, fix commits 2026-04-16, GHSA-ff2p-hmqr-hxm4; CVE-2026-34780 (8.3 HIGH): context-isolation bypass via bridged WebCodecs VideoFrame objects. (b) PROCESS/PRIVILEGE CONFIGURATION — CVE-2026-34769 (7.7 HIGH): an undocumented commandLineSwitches webPreference lets switches be appended to the renderer command line, potentially disabling renderer sandboxing, when webPreferences is built by spreading untrusted config; CVE-2026-34775 (6.8): nodeIntegrationInWorker not correctly scoped in shared renderer processes, so workers in frames set to false could still receive Node.js integration. (c) IPC INTEGRITY — CVE-2026-34778 (5.9): a service worker can spoof reply messages on the internal IPC channel used by webContents.executeJavaScript(), resolving the main-process promise with attacker-controlled data. Why this matters to the argument: CVE-2026-70610 is prototype pollution crossing the context-isolation boundary, which is the missing link between the ledger's Node.js prototype-pollution line (Silent Spring, GHunter, Bullseye, UoP) and Electron proper — the pollution primitive those papers study, landing in Electron's own C++ bridge. And CVE-2026-70601 is a near-repeat of CVE-2023-29198 (contextBridge context-isolation bypass), supporting a recurrence/regression framing. Also closes the 08-07 open item: that run recorded an unverified search-summary claim about CVE-2026-70601; it is now confirmed against GLAD + the Electron GHSA references.

CVE-2026-70601.title: Context isolation bypass via Function.prototype.bind hijack

CVE-2026-70610.cwe: CWE-1321 (Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes / Prototype Pollution)
CVE-2026-70610.title: contextBridge object copy honors prototype setters
CVE-2026-70610.advisory_text_verbatim: Objects copied across the contextBridge boundary from untrusted content could carry an attacker-influenced prototype, enabling prototype-pollution-style attacks against preload code despite context isolation being enabled. Apps are only affected if their preload code accepts object arguments from untrusted content and reads properties from them without own-property checks. Apps that only accept primitive arguments, or that validate object arguments, are not affected.
CVE-2026-70610.exploitation_precondition: Preload code must accept OBJECT arguments from untrusted content and read properties WITHOUT own-property checks (hasOwnProperty / Object.hasOwn). Primitive-only or validating preloads are unaffected. This is the most thesis-relevant sentence in the whole 2026 advisory set: it defines, in the framework maintainers' own words, the exact preload coding pattern that turns prototype pollution into a context-isolation bypass - i.e. a concrete, checkable detection predicate for any static/dynamic Electron analysis.

CVE-2026-34780.title: Context Isolation bypass via contextBridge VideoFrame transfer

CVE-2026-34769.title: Renderer command-line switch injection via undocumented commandLineSwitches webPreference

CVE-2026-34775.title: nodeIntegrationInWorker not correctly scoped in shared renderer processes

CVE-2026-34778.title: Service worker can spoof executeJavaScript IPC replies

CVE-2026-70598.title: Off-screen rendering trusts GPU-supplied geometry over shared-memory size
CVE-2026-70598.detail: In offscreen rendering mode the MAIN process does not validate that the byte count implied by the GPU-supplied frame geometry fits the received shared-memory buffer, so a compromised GPU process makes the main process read out-of-bounds while producing 'paint' event images - memory disclosure or crash. Only affects apps using webPreferences.offscreen, and requires the attacker to already hold code execution in the GPU process (hence LOW). Note the CVSS scope change (S:C): the bug is a PROCESS-BOUNDARY trust failure that is NOT the renderer<->main IPC channel.

CVE-2026-34764.title: Use-after-free in offscreen shared texture release() callback
CVE-2026-34764.detail: The release() callback handed to app code on a 'paint' event texture can outlive its backing native state; invoking it afterwards dereferences freed memory IN THE MAIN PROCESS (crash or memory corruption). Only affects webPreferences.offscreen: { useSharedTexture: true }. Workaround: call texture.release() promptly before the texture object becomes unreachable. IMPORTANT LEDGER FIX: this GHSA was published 2026-04-03, which finally dates the CVE-2026-34764..34781 batch (an 08-08 open item recorded as unconfirmed) - the two 2026 batches are therefore APRIL (34764..34781) and AUGUST (70597..70612), not one August disclosure.

CVE-2026-70605.severity: MODERATE (per the third-party summary; CVSS not verified)
CVE-2026-70605.title: net.fetch() / net.request() follow redirects to file:// and other local resources
CVE-2026-70605.detail: Reported to affect how Electron's net.fetch() and net.request() APIs handle HTTP redirects: a remote server can answer with a redirect pointing at a file:// URL or another local resource, and the MAIN process follows it. This would be a FOURTH trust boundary in the 2026 taxonomy - remote web server -> main process via Electron's own networking API - distinct from (a) contextBridge, (b) renderer<->main IPC / process configuration, and (c) GPU -> main. context_non_venue.venue: Open-source tooling (GitHub) + GitHub Blog; MIT-licensed, published on PyPI
context_non_venue.scope_topical: ADJACENT (agentic vulnerability-discovery tooling) — prior-art check for a discovery thesis, not a paper
context_non_venue.why: OPENED IN RESPONSE TO THE 08-30 TOP PRIORITY, AND THE ANSWER IS FAVOURABLE TO THE THESIS. The Vikunja advisory (CVE-2026-33334, GHSA-xh67-63q3-hf7g) credits its discovery to 'GitHub Security Lab Taskflows', making it the only tool-attributed find in the whole corpus; every other advisory here is credited to a named human. The 08-30 entry flagged the open question: is this a general scanner that happened to catch an Electron config, or does it ship an Electron-specific taskflow? PRIMARY-SOURCE ANSWER: it is GENERAL. The repo README (read in full) describes 'example taskflows to use with the SecLab Taskflow Agent, as well as the custom MCP servers that are needed to run the taskflows' — an 'experimental agentic framework' used 'as a code auditing tool' with a CodeQL MCP server, run over a whole repository (the documented demo targets are github/cmark-gfm and OWASP Juice Shop) and writing results to an SQLite 'audit_result' table with a 'has_vulnerability' column. Two repos: seclab-taskflow-agent (the engine) and seclab-taskflows (the suite). Nothing in the README, and nothing surfaced by a targeted search, names Electron, nodeIntegration, contextIsolation, preload or contextBridge. THE SHARPEST FINDING, AND A GENUINE TENSION WORTH CITING: the triage taskflow src/seclab_taskflows/taskflows/audit/classify_application_local.yaml (read in full at commit 4d8c3db) instructs the model TWICE, verbatim, to exclude exactly the finding class the Vikunja CVE consists of — 'take care not to include issues that are of low severity or requires unrealistic attack scenario such as misconfiguration' and 'do not include issues that requires system to be already compromised, such as issues that relies on maliciious [sic] configurations, stolen credentials, misconfiguration etc.' So the framework whose output produced a CVE FOR A webPreferences CONFIG ALONE carries a prompt that tells the agent misconfigurations are not reportable. WHY THIS MATTERS: (1) PRIOR ART IS BOUNDED — the strongest agentic competitor now visible is a general-purpose repo auditor with no Electron model, no notion of renderer/main process boundaries and no webPreferences awareness, so an Electron-specialised discovery method is not pre-empted; (2) it is direct evidence for the thesis's own framing that generic auditing pipelines systematically DEPRIORITISE the Electron config class, which is precisely why that class keeps recurring in the advisory record (SiYuan nine-plus, Vikunja, DeepChat, DbGate, Notesnook); (3) the same YAML does list 'remote web request or IPC, RPC calls' among untrusted-input sources, so the vocabulary is present even though the Electron specialisation is not — a natural place to argue a contribution. CAVEATS: classify_application_local.yaml is ONE taskflow of many and was read at a pinned commit, not at main; the audit/ directory listing could NOT be enumerated (GitHub tree views are React-rendered and return empty to web_fetch), so other taskflows in that directory remain unread; and it is NOT established that the Vikunja find came from this particular taskflow.

context_non_venue.venue: GitHub Security Advisories, siyuan-note/siyuan repository (vendor-published)
context_non_venue.scope_topical: PRIMARY (XSS→RCE in a real Electron desktop app, exactly the thesis vulnerability class) — but vendor advisories, not peer-reviewed academic work
context_non_venue.why: The best single-application longitudinal case study this watch has found, and the application-level counterpart to the already-ledgered upstream-Electron CVE entry (which covers the FRAMEWORK's own bugs). SiYuan is a personal knowledge-management app (siyuan-note/siyuan, ~45.5k GitHub stars) whose Electron desktop client ships an insecure renderer profile, and the vendor has now published EIGHT XSS-to-RCE advisories against that same profile without ever changing it. Two were read in full from the primary GHSA pages this run: (a) GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 / CVE-2026-39846 — STORED XSS in synced table captions: the table `caption` attribute is saved into the node's IAL properties without HTML escaping, then read back, HTML-UNescaped, and written into the rendered DOM; delivery is a crafted `.sy.zip` note imported into a shared sync target, so the victim is compromised simply by syncing and opening the note. Because the renderer runs `nodeIntegration: true` / `contextIsolation: false`, the payload `` executes as OS code. (b) GHSA-6gx2-8gcr-x83f — REFLECTED XSS to OS RCE via the `siyuan://` deep link, with a file-and-line-level root-cause chain that is unusually citable: `app/electron/main.js:81,84` registers `setAsDefaultProtocolClient("siyuan")`; the received URL is fanned out with NO allowlist or sanitizer to every workspace window via `workspaces.forEach(item => item.browserWindow.webContents.send("siyuan-open-url", url))` (main.js:1692-1696; macOS `open-url` 1675-1697; argv scan 568-577); the renderer picks it up at `app/src/boot/onGetConfig.ts:168` (`ipcRenderer.on(Constants.SIYUAN_OPEN_URL, ...)`); `processSiYuanUriBazaar` (`app/src/util/uri.ts:100-127`) `decodeURIComponent`s the path segment at line 107 with no allowlist, no length cap and no escapeHtml; `openBazaarReadme` (`app/src/config/index.ts:88-134`) feeds it verbatim into `showMessage(`Package not found: ${itemName}`)`; and `app/src/dialog/message.ts:73,84` writes it with `insertAdjacentHTML` (two further sinks at lines 44-51 and 59). THIS IS THE THESIS-USABLE PART: the advisory states that every `BrowserWindow` in the app is configured `nodeIntegration:true, webviewTag:true, webSecurity:false, contextIsolation:false`, with `@electron/remote` enabled globally, `--disable-web-security` set on the command line (main.js:87), and `content-security-policy` / `x-frame-options` / `access-control-allow-origin` STRIPPED from every response (main.js:554-565) — 'There is no CSP, no SOP, no origin isolation.' It then names the seven prior XSS-to-RCE advisories filed against that identical profile — GHSA-pcjq-j3mq-jv5j, GHSA-27qc-m5gf-jv5r, GHSA-mvjr-vv3c-w4qv, GHSA-ff66-236v-p4fg, GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2, GHSA-grjj-6f6g-cq8q, GHSA-2h64-c999-c9r6 — and observes, verbatim: 'Each has been fixed at the sink, never at the profile.' It adds that `showMessage` is the shared sink for roughly 20 sibling reflection paths, so a per-call escape leaves the siblings live. WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE ARGUMENT: (1) it is a documented, primary-sourced, eight-times-repeated instance of the exact escalation the thesis is about (DOM/XSS sink → Node.js privilege → OS command execution), i.e. motivation with a recurrence curve rather than a single anecdote; (2) it is direct empirical support for the claim that per-sink patching does not close the class while the webPreferences profile is unsafe — the argument for tooling that audits the PROFILE (Inspectron) or defends the ESCALATION (COINDEF) rather than individual sinks; (3) the deep-link path (OS protocol handler → main process → unsanitized broadcast over renderer IPC → DOM sink) is a concrete, real-world instance of a cross-process message-progression chain, i.e. field evidence for the bug class Proton / 'Buzz to Boom' defines; and (4) the advisory's own recommended fix — `contextIsolation:true, sandbox:true, nodeIntegration:false, webSecurity:true` plus a `contextBridge` preload exposing only the required Node subset, and deleting both `--disable-web-security` and the header-strip block — is a clean statement of the secure-baseline the thesis can measure real apps against.

CVE-2026-50551.title_verbatim: Stored XSS to RCE via Unsanitized Attribute View Asset Cell Content

CVE-2026-50551.cvss_note: UI:N (no user interaction). Every other advisory in the corpus is UI:R. Sink 1 fires on page load, so merely opening a synced note is sufficient — this is why it outscores the 9.6 deep-link advisory.

CVE-2026-50551.source_verbatim: app/src/protyle/render/av/asset.ts:405 — addAssetLink() reads user input from a free-form <textarea> with no sanitization. Kernel stores MAsset.Content raw (kernel/av/value.go:53), no server-side sanitization.
CVE-2026-50551.sink_1_verbatim: DIRECT STORED XSS, triggers on page load. app/src/protyle/render/av/cell.ts:1008 emits `>${item.name || item.content}` — raw user input with zero escaping. app/src/protyle/render/av/blockAttr.ts:93 is worse still, completely unescaped: ``. Rendered via action.ts:860 `cellElement.innerHTML = renderCell(...)`.
CVE-2026-50551.sink_2_verbatim: HOVER-TRIGGERED XSS VIA ARIA-LABEL ROUND-TRIP. Same lines emit `aria-label="${escapeAttr(item.content)}"` on .ariaLabel elements. escapeAttr() (util/escape.ts:14) escapes only " and ' — NOT < or >. popover.ts:33 global mouseover handler reads aria-label via getAttribute (which attribute-DECODES entities); line 144 calls showTooltip(decodeURIComponent(tip), ...); tooltip.ts:41 does `messageElement.innerHTML = message`.

Advisory: 'In a sync/collaboration scenario, the malicious note propagates to all users.' Persistence: 'malicious payload stored in .sy files, executes on every open.'
CVE-2026-50551.incomplete_fix_pattern_verbatim: 'This is a neighbor-bug of CVE-2026-44588: the fix for -44588 used escapeAriaLabel() (double-escapes <), but the AV asset renderers were left using the weaker escapeAttr() (escapes only quotes) or no escaping at all.' newly_named_prior_advisories: CVE-2026-44588 / GHSA-25rp-h46x-2hjm (the parent bug this one neighbours)

CVE-2026-44588.title_verbatim_glad: SiYuan: Electron Renderer RCE via decodeURIComponent-driven tooltip XSS in aria-label sink (incomplete fix for CVE-2026-34585)
CVE-2026-44588.cvss_note: PR:N — no privileges required, unlike CVE-2026-50551 (PR:L) and CVE-2026-33066 (PR:L). Same 9.6 total as -33066 but reached by a different route.
CVE-2026-44588.cwe_note: FIRST advisory in this corpus to carry CWE-1188 'Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default' ALONGSIDE the XSS CWE. That is the webPreferences profile itself being assigned a weakness class inside an advisory that also has a concrete sink — i.e. the (A1) config+sink case getting the CWE that Vikunja's (A2) config-alone case earned on its own. Useful for arguing the two are the same finding at different levels of completeness.
CVE-2026-44588.glad_record_dates: GitLab Advisory Database record dated May 8, 2026, updated May 15, 2026. These are GLAD record dates, NOT the GHSA publication date — the GHSA page itself was not opened.
CVE-2026-44588.privilege_config_verbatim: app/electron/main.js:407-411 — nodeIntegration: true, contextIsolation: false, webSecurity: false
CVE-2026-44588.privilege_config_note: NOTE THE LINE DRIFT AND THE THIRD FLAG. The identical profile is cited at main.js:307 in CVE-2026-50551, at main.js:422-426 in CVE-2026-33066, and at main.js:407-411 here — three different line ranges across three advisories written against three different versions. THESIS POINT: line-anchored detection of this profile is fragile; pattern-anchored detection is not. Also, this is the first entry in this key_advisories map to record webSecurity: false explicitly alongside the other two flags (GHSA-6gx2-8gcr-x83f already reported it at the app-wide level).
CVE-2026-44588.mechanism_verbatim: The producer-side encoder escapeAriaLabel (app/src/util/escape.ts:19-25) 'only handles HTML special characters (", ', <, literal <) — it leaves %XX URL-escapes untouched.' A doc title containing %3Cimg src=x onerror=...%3E therefore round-trips through escapeAriaLabel and the HTML attribute layer unmodified. The consumer, the tooltip mouseover handler in app/src/block/popover.ts, reads aria-label via getAttribute and passes it through decodeURIComponent before assigning to messageElement.innerHTML at app/src/dialog/tooltip.ts:41. decodeURIComponent turns %3C into a LITERAL < (not a character reference), so the HTML5 tokenizer enters TagOpenState, parses the , and onerror fires. require('child_process') is then reachable from the injected handler.
CVE-2026-44588.escalation_primitive: (vii) ENCODER/DECODER LAYER MISMATCH — distinct from the (vi) sanitizer/decode-path mismatch recorded for CVE-2026-50551. Here the escaper is HTML-aware and the attacker simply uses a DIFFERENT alphabet (percent-encoding) that the escaper does not model, which a later decodeURIComponent converts back. -50551's sink 2 fails because entity decoding undoes a correct quote-escape; -44588 fails because URL decoding introduces syntax the escaper never saw. Both defeat sanitizer-aware taint analysis, but a tool would need two different checks to catch them.
CVE-2026-44588.reachable_sources_verbatim: 'Doc titles, AV column names + descriptions, AV select options, file-tree tooltips all reach this sink because they're rendered into class="ariaLabel" elements with aria-label="${escapeAriaLabel(...)}".' Doc title is named as the easiest plant — 'any user with create/rename access lands the payload, and the file survives .sy.zip round-trip without modification.'
CVE-2026-44588.affected_glad: All versions up to 0.0.0-20260421031503-96dfe0bea474 (Go pseudo-version, gomod ecosystem view)
